stem: After a fall, an older adult has severe hip pain, cannot bear weight, and the affected leg appears shortened and externally rotated. What should the nurse suspect?

options.A: Expected post-fall soreness because a visible change in leg position does not suggest skeletal injury.
options.B: An uncomplicated muscle strain because shortening and external rotation are typical after a minor soft-tissue injury.
options.C: A lumbar strain because hip fractures generally do not cause inability to bear weight or lower-extremity deformity.
options.D: A hip fracture that requires prompt medical evaluation and diagnostic imaging rather than assuming a simple bruise or strain.

rationale: NCBI StatPearls describes the classic presentation of a displaced hip fracture as pain and immobility with a shortened, externally rotated limb; hip fractures commonly occur in older adults after a fall. Most can be identified on plain radiographs. The combination in the stem should therefore prompt suspicion for hip fracture and diagnostic evaluation. A through C do not account for the characteristic deformity and inability to bear weight.
educational_objective: Recognize severe hip pain, inability to bear weight, and a shortened externally rotated leg after a fall as findings strongly suggestive of hip fracture requiring prompt evaluation.
source_organization: National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI Bookshelf)
source_version_date: Last update August 8, 2023; accessed and currentness-rechecked 2026-08-16
source_locator: History and Physical — classic shortened and externally rotated limb; Evaluation — majority of hip fractures diagnosed on plain-film radiographs
source_claim_supported: Hip fracture after a fall commonly presents with pain/immobility and may produce a shortened, externally rotated limb; diagnostic evaluation generally includes radiography.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Printed p.14, Physiological Adaptation — recognize and manage acute alterations in body systems and complications of injury
blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — recognition of hip fracture after a fall

source_original.stem: After a fall, an older adult has severe hip pain, cannot bear weight, and the affected leg appears shortened and externally rotated. What should the nurse suspect?

options.A: Normal post-fall soreness because visible leg-position change does not suggest skeletal injury
options.B: Uncomplicated muscle strain because shortening and external rotation are expected after minor falls
options.C: Lumbar strain because hip fractures do not usually interfere with weight bearing after a fall
options.D: Hip fracture requiring prompt evaluation and imaging rather than assuming a simple soft-tissue bruise

source_original.rationale: Hip fracture should be strongly suspected after a fall when there is hip/groin pain, inability to bear weight, and characteristic deformity such as shortening and external rotation. Imaging is required to confirm the diagnosis.
source_original.source_detail: Symptoms/signs and diagnosis of hip fracture after falls in older adults, including external rotation/shortening and inability to bear weight; accessed 2026-08-14.

correction_summary: Replaced the secondary Merck source with NCBI StatPearls per source hierarchy, retained the classic finding cluster and need for diagnostic imaging, and reduced difficulty from hard to easy because this is direct pattern recognition.

audit_findings.currentness: NCBI chapter last updated 2023; current search found no conflicting newer authoritative diagnostic description, and the classic presentation remains unchanged.
audit_findings.claim_audit: NCBI directly supports pain/immobility, shortened external rotation, suspicion of hip fracture, and plain-radiograph evaluation.

distractor_audit.A: Deformity plus inability to bear weight is not expected simple soreness.
distractor_audit.B: Shortening/external rotation suggests displaced fracture rather than simple strain.
distractor_audit.C: Does not explain characteristic hip deformity and inability to bear weight.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Posterior hip dislocation can also prevent weight bearing but classically produces internal rather than external rotation; the final finding cluster makes D uniquely best.
audit_findings.cueing: All choices are post-fall musculoskeletal interpretations; answer requires recognizing the pattern.
audit_findings.blueprint: Physiological Adaptation is appropriate for acute injury recognition and management.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Re-solved the item, compared hip fracture with hip dislocation and soft-tissue injury patterns, rechecked NCBI History/Physical and Evaluation, and confirmed D remained uniquely correct.
